authors: Ryan, J. et al. (Irish Council for Civil Liberties, Enforce unit)
title: 5 years: GDPR's crisis point - ICCL's 2023 report on EEA data protection authorities
method: descriptive analysis of the EDPB register of Article 60 one-stop-shop final decisions and DPA budget data
outcomes: cross-border enforcement measures; share of Irish DPC decisions overruled; DPA budgets
headline: By late 2022, 63% of the 160 EU-level enforcement measures in the EDPB register were mere reprimands, and 67% of the Irish DPC's investigation decisions in EU cases were overruled by majority vote of other DPAs (figures as revised 31 May 2023).
summary_plain: A civil liberties group counted the decisions taken in Europe-wide privacy cases in the first five years of the GDPR. It found that most ended in a reprimand rather than a fine, and that Ireland's regulator, which oversees most big tech firms, was often overruled by its EU peers who wanted tougher action.
quality: Descriptive counts from official register; no counterfactual; author is a campaigning NGO; figures revised after publication
interested_party: Campaigning NGO (ICCL Enforce) litigating against the Irish DPC and big tech

authors: Chivot, E. & Castro, D. (Center for Data Innovation / ITIF)
title: What the Evidence Shows About the Impact of the GDPR After One Year
venue: Center for Data Innovation, Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF)
method: compilation of early post-GDPR evidence (surveys, web measurements, market data, press reports)
outcomes: business costs, startups, ad-tech competition, user trust, online access, regulator resources
headline: Reviewing the first year of evidence, the authors conclude the GDPR drains company resources, hurts EU tech startups, reduces competition in digital advertising, fails to raise user trust and strains regulators.
summary_plain: A US tech-policy think tank gathered the early data and reports on what happened in the GDPR's first year. It argues the law imposed large costs, helped big ad firms against smaller ones and did not make people trust the internet more.
quality: Selective secondary compilation of early, mostly descriptive evidence; advocacy framing; no own causal analysis
interested_party: ITIF is funded partly by large tech firms and has opposed the GDPR model

title: Why the EU right to consent to personal data processing doesn't work
method: structured review of empirical evidence on GDPR consent tools and their private and social welfare effects
outcomes: consent rates, dark patterns, data-broker concentration, app exits, prices
headline: Drawing on post-2018 studies (e.g. a 15% fall in third-party data brokers used by websites and a 17% rise in concentration among those retained after GDPR), the paper concludes GDPR consent banners are 'a legal and technical fiction': few consent tools are fully compliant and reduced data sharing carries social costs.
summary_plain: A Bruegel economist reviews what has happened with cookie-consent pop-ups since the GDPR. He finds that people click through them to save time, many banners are designed to push acceptance, and the rules have also cost the economy through fewer data firms and app exits.
quality: Evidence synthesis of existing studies, no new data; written for a debate panel; extracts a forthcoming Bruegel paper (Mariniello et al. 2026)

authors: Decarolis, F. & Firullo, C. (published with Clifford Chance LLP)
title: Unlocking growth: exploring the economic impact of GDPR for tomorrow's Europe
venue: Clifford Chance thought leadership (funded by Amazon)
method: systematic synthesis of empirical literature plus structured interviews and closed questionnaires with industry experts (multinationals, ad-tech, startups)
outcomes: compliance costs, data costs, cross-border data flows, VC investment, innovation, user welfare, DPA fragmentation
headline: The review concludes the GDPR raised formal privacy standards 'at a significant and uneven economic cost': substantial recurrent compliance costs, higher data acquisition costs, reduced cross-border data flows and a measurable slowdown in VC investment and innovation in data-driven industries.
summary_plain: Two academics, paid for by Amazon and published by a law firm, pulled together the research on the GDPR's economic effects and interviewed company experts. They conclude the law improved privacy rules on paper but cost firms a lot and slowed investment and innovation.
quality: Literature synthesis plus small, non-random expert interviews; industry-funded; no new causal estimates
interested_party: Funded by Amazon (subject to GDPR); published with Clifford Chance

title: Fünf Jahre DS-GVO: Unternehmen sind weiterhin verunsichert (survey of 602 companies)
method: representative survey of 602 German companies with 20+ employees
outcomes: innovation projects stopped, hesitation to use data
headline: 60% of German firms said they had stopped innovation plans at least once because of data-protection rules or uncertainty, and 62% hesitate to use data for fear of breaching data protection; a 2025 wave of 605 firms reported 70% (61% in 2024).
summary_plain: Germany's digital industry association asks firms every year how the GDPR affects them. A growing majority say they have dropped new projects because of privacy rules or unclear interpretations.
quality: Self-reported perceptions from an industry-association survey; no counterfactual; 2025 figure taken from zm-online report of the Bitkom release
interested_party: Industry association lobbying for GDPR simplification

authors: Berggren, H. (National Board of Trade Sweden / Kommerskollegium)
title: The GDPR and international trade - evidence and implications for EU policy
venue: Kommerskollegium (Swedish National Board of Trade) analysis
method: review of empirical studies and industry reports on GDPR, trade and productivity
outcomes: cross-border data flows, compliance costs, productivity, trade competitiveness
headline: Based on empirical studies and industry reports, the agency concludes the GDPR has hindered EU companies' productivity and international competitiveness by creating regulatory uncertainty, raising compliance costs and reducing data storage and processing.
summary_plain: Sweden's trade agency reviewed the research on the GDPR and trade. It finds the law spread EU privacy standards worldwide but made data flows harder and costlier, hurting EU firms' productivity and trade.
quality: Evidence review by a national authority, no new estimates; policy-oriented (recommends revision)

title: Coordinated Enforcement Action: Implementation of the right of access by controllers (CEF 2024 report)
method: coordinated investigations and questionnaires by 30 DPAs; 1,185 responding controllers
outcomes: compliance with the right of access
headline: Of 1,185 controllers examined by 30 DPAs in 2024, two thirds of DPAs rated compliance with the right of access 'average' to 'high', but seven recurring problems were found (e.g. no documented procedures, excessive ID demands, over-broad refusals), with larger controllers more compliant than small ones.
summary_plain: Europe's privacy regulators jointly checked how well organisations answer people's requests to see their personal data. Most do reasonably well, especially big ones, but many lack proper procedures or put obstacles in people's way.
quality: Large official compliance exercise; mixed methods across DPAs, non-random samples, self-reported answers
interested_party: Regulators assessing compliance with the law they enforce

title: Coordinated Enforcement Action: Designation and Position of Data Protection Officers (CEF 2023 report)
method: coordinated investigations by 25 DPAs with more than 17,000 questionnaire replies from organisations and DPOs
headline: Based on more than 17,000 replies across the EEA five years after GDPR, most DPOs report adequate skills, defined tasks and being consulted, but 'too many' lack designation where mandatory, resources, independence or reporting lines to top management.
summary_plain: Regulators surveyed over 17,000 organisations and their data protection officers. Most officers say they can do their job, but a sizeable group are missing, under-resourced or not independent.
quality: Very large official survey; self-reported, samples chosen by each DPA
interested_party: Regulators assessing compliance with the law they enforce

title: Deutsche Industrie sieht Data Act als Chance - aber es gibt noch viel zu tun (survey of 400 industry executives)
venue: HPE-commissioned YouGov survey, reported by it-daily.net
method: survey of 400 executives in German industrial firms (YouGov, March 2024)
outcomes: perceptions and preparation for the Data Act
headline: Two thirds (67%) of German industrial firms saw the Data Act more as an opportunity than a risk, and 43% had started preparing for it, about 18 months before it applied.
summary_plain: A survey of German manufacturers after the Data Act was adopted found most saw it as a chance to use machine data, but fewer than half had started getting ready.
quality: Readiness/perception survey before application; commissioned by a vendor; only secondary press report available
interested_party: Commissioned by HPE, a data-infrastructure vendor that benefits from Data Act compliance demand

title: MiCA: The end of the transitional period for CASPs - What comes after 1 July 2026?
method: descriptive tabulation of the ESMA interim MiCA register
outcomes: number and location of authorised CASPs
headline: As of June 2026 about 216 firms had MiCA authorisation versus more than 1,200 crypto service providers previously registered under national AML regimes, concentrated in Germany (55), the Netherlands (26) and France (19).
summary_plain: A consultancy counted how many crypto firms had obtained the new EU licence just before the transition period ended. Only about one in six of the previously registered firms had done so, mostly in a few countries.
quality: Simple descriptive counts from official register; marketing piece for Cyprus

title: Kaiko/Bitvavo report on crypto trading in Europe (MiCA-compliant stablecoins dominate European market)
method: descriptive analysis of exchange trading data
outcomes: euro crypto trading volumes; euro stablecoin market shares and volumes
headline: After MiCA's stablecoin rules applied (June 2024), MiCA-compliant coins captured most of the euro-stablecoin market, while monthly euro-stablecoin volumes exceeded $300 million through 2024 (peak near $800 million in November) and Tether discontinued EURT.
summary_plain: A crypto data firm found that once MiCA rules began, euro stablecoins that met the rules took over most of their market as exchanges dropped non-compliant coins.
quality: Descriptive industry data; no counterfactual; primary report not accessible, figures from press coverage
interested_party: Bitvavo is a crypto exchange subject to MiCA; Kaiko sells market data

authors: Bindseil, U. & Voloder, E. (Blockchain for Europe)
title: Reforming MiCA for Euro Stablecoins
method: structured qualitative assessment of MiCA e-money-token rules with market data (DeFiLlama) and international comparison
outcomes: euro stablecoin competitiveness, reserve rules, remuneration ban
headline: The report argues MiCA has made euro stablecoins safe but commercially weak, citing data that euro stablecoins remain under 1% of global stablecoin volume against a dollar-stablecoin market above $300 billion.
summary_plain: A crypto industry group, with a former ECB official, argues that MiCA's strict rules on reserves and the ban on paying interest have kept euro stablecoins tiny next to dollar ones.
quality: Advocacy-oriented assessment with light descriptive data; no causal analysis
interested_party: Industry association of blockchain firms lobbying for MiCA reform

authors: Gardner, H., Enzerink, S., Page, M., Brincat, A. (Capgemini); Tenge, E., Velcsov, T., Macchioni, M.S. (Spark Legal and Policy Consulting); Lechardoy, L., Spolverato, G. (Open Evidence)
title: Study supporting the evaluation of the Free Flow of Non-Personal Data Regulation, Open Data Directive and Data Governance Act - Final Report
venue: European Commission, DG CONNECT (Publications Office, published January 2026)
method: ex-post evaluation: legal analysis, stakeholder surveys, interviews and consultations
outcomes: public sector data supply and reuse; high-value datasets implementation
headline: The evaluation finds the Open Data Directive has successfully catalysed public sector data supply and reuse, although implementation of High-Value Datasets remains uneven and technical fragmentation persists.
summary_plain: The Commission's contracted evaluation says the open data law has led governments to publish and share more data, but the key 'high-value' datasets are not yet published consistently across countries.
quality: Official ex-post evaluation; mainly qualitative/stakeholder evidence, no counterfactual (the same study is listed for the Free Flow Regulation under the name Open Evidence et al.)
interested_party: Commissioned and steered by the Commission (evaluating its own act)

authors: Ramponi, M., Moro, M., Suárez, J. (data.europa.eu)
title: High-value Datasets Best Practices Report
venue: data.europa.eu / Publications Office of the EU (DOI 10.2830/113131)
method: qualitative interviews with representatives of seven Member States
headline: Interviews with seven Member States around the HVD Regulation's start (9 June 2024) found varying degrees of adoption, difficulties making some HVDs free of charge and significant obstacles to using EU vocabularies, APIs and bulk downloads.
summary_plain: An EU open-data portal study asked seven countries how they were coping with the new duty to publish key datasets for free. Progress varied, and some found the technical and free-of-charge rules hard to meet.

authors: European Data Protection Supervisor (national report in EDPB CEF 2024 annex)
title: EDPS report on the right of access in EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (Coordinated Enforcement Framework 2024, Appendix: national reports)
method: survey of all 75 EUIs (63 responded) plus complaint-handling records 2023-mid 2024, DPO activity reports and a DPO workshop
outcomes: volume and handling of data subject access requests under Regulation 2018/1725
headline: 58 of 63 responding EU institutions and agencies received only 0-25 access requests in 2023; the EDPS found decentralised handling, difficulty distinguishing access requests from other requests, and excessive identity checks.
summary_plain: The EU's own privacy watchdog checked how EU bodies deal with people asking for their personal data. Few such requests arrive, but many bodies lack central systems and some ask for too much identification.
quality: Official census-type survey with descriptive statistics; qualitative findings from supervisor's own case work
interested_party: Supervisor assessing compliance with the law it enforces

searched: 2 web searches (Portability Regulation evaluation, BEUC, EAO, EPRS implementation appraisal, usage surveys 2023-24); only items already listed (Commission 2022 report, Visionary Analytics study, Flash EB 477a, EAO 2019) surfaced; no think tank assessments
1 web search (noyb, EDRi, BEUC, CEPS on Regulation 2025/2518); only law-firm explainers; the act applies from April 2027 so no ex-post evidence exists yet

2 web searches (ECIPE/OECD data localisation after 2019; Commission Art. 8 evaluation report); only pre-2019 ECIPE estimates and the existing evaluation study; one 2025 Spanish legal article on AEPD resolutions (Argelich Comelles, RCDI 812) is legal analysis without reported findings, so excluded

3 web searches (civil society/FRA/Statewatch LED assessments, empirical police DPO studies, FRA 2026 LED-in-practice report); EDRi shadow evaluation and EDPB contribution already listed; FRA report only previewed (preliminary findings May 2026), not yet published

2 web searches (ETUI, Bruegel, EPC, Fairwork transposition assessments; post-adoption reclassification evidence, Eurofound); only law-firm/vendor transposition trackers and Spain's 2021 Riders' Law studies (a national predecessor, not the directive); transposition deadline is Dec 2026
